title: The 10-Point Website Audit Checklist for Business Owners
excerpt: A practical checklist any business owner can run in under an hour — no developer required. Find out what's holding your website back.

blocks.text: Most business owners only look at their website when something is obviously broken. A form stops working. A page goes blank. The phone stops ringing.
By that point, you've already lost visitors. The damage is done.

A website audit doesn't require a developer or a €5,000 agency report. These 10 checks take under an hour, use free tools, and will surface the problems most likely to be costing you leads and revenue right now.
Work through this list once a quarter. Bookmark it.
1. Speed (Mobile First)
Go to **PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev) and enter your URL. Run it for mobile first — mobile is how Google measures you, and it's where most of your visitors arrive.

rows: Good — you're likely not losing customers to speed
Needs work — you're losing some visitors
Urgent — this is actively hurting your business

blocks.text: The metric that matters most: **Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)**. This is how long it takes your main content to appear. Under 2.5 seconds is good. Over 4 seconds is a serious problem.
If your score is below 50, screenshot the "Opportunities" section at the bottom of the report. That's your to-do list.
For context: well-optimised Next.js sites typically score 90–98 on mobile. The average WordPress site without dedicated optimisation scores 40–65.
2. Core Web Vitals
Core Web Vitals are Google's official measure of user experience. They are a confirmed ranking factor — poor scores mean lower positions in search results, regardless of how good your content is.
Three metrics to check:

items: **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint):** How fast does the main content load? Goal: under 2.5s
**INP (Interaction to Next Paint):** How quickly does the page respond to clicks and taps? Goal: under 200ms
**CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift):** Does content jump around as the page loads? Goal: under 0.1

blocks.text: PageSpeed Insights shows all three. Google Search Console also has a Core Web Vitals report once your site is registered.
Failed Core Web Vitals means lower rankings. There is no workaround — Google's algorithm penalises pages that fail these benchmarks.
3. Mobile Responsiveness
Pull out your phone and browse your own website as if you were a customer.
Ask yourself:

items: Is the text readable without zooming?
Can you tap buttons and links without hitting the wrong one?
Does the navigation work cleanly?
Are images displayed correctly, or are they cropped or overflowing?
Can you find your contact details or contact form within 30 seconds?

blocks.text: More than 60% of web traffic is now mobile. If the experience is poor on a phone, you are losing the majority of your visitors.
Also test on a tablet if your audience is likely to use one. Tablet layouts are a common blind spot — they often look broken in ways that phone or desktop views don't reveal.
4. SSL Certificate
Check that your site loads at **https://** (not http://) and shows a padlock icon in the browser address bar.

If you see "Not Secure", your visitors see it too. That warning kills trust immediately — many users will leave before they read a single word. Chrome and Firefox also actively warn users before loading pages without SSL.
SSL certificates are free via Let's Encrypt and should be automatically provided by any modern hosting platform. If your host isn't doing this, that's a signal to upgrade your hosting.
5. Contact Forms and Calls to Action
Go through your website as a new customer trying to get in touch. Fill in your contact form. Did you receive the email? Did the confirmation message appear?
Broken contact forms are more common than you'd expect — and the people who encounter them don't tell you. They just leave and contact a competitor.
Also check:

items: Is your phone number a clickable tel: link on mobile?
Is your email a clickable mailto: link?
Is your main CTA ("Book a call", "Get a quote", "Contact us") visible above the fold on mobile without scrolling?

blocks.text: Every extra step or friction point between a visitor and your contact form costs you enquiries. The goal is to make contacting you effortless.
6. Meta Titles and Descriptions

Your meta title is the blue clickable link in Google search results. Your meta description is the two-line snippet below it. These are essentially your advertising copy in Google — and most business owners have never touched them.
To check yours, right-click any page and choose "View Page Source". Search for `<title>` and `<meta name="description">`. Or use the free browser extension "SEO Meta in 1 Click".
Every page should have:

items: A unique title (not the same generic title on every page)
A title under 60 characters — longer gets truncated in search results
A description under 155 characters that explains the page and makes someone want to click
Your primary keyword in the title of relevant pages

blocks.text: If your homepage title is just your company name, you're missing an opportunity. "Webvise — Fast Business Websites in Next.js" tells Google and searchers something useful. "Webvise" tells them nothing.
7. Google Search Console
Google Search Console is free and essential. If you haven't set it up, do it now — it takes about 15 minutes.
Once registered, check these four reports:

items: **Coverage:** Are any pages returning errors (404, 500)? Are important pages excluded from Google's index?
**Core Web Vitals:** Which pages fail Google's speed benchmarks?
**Search Results:** What queries are bringing visitors? Which pages rank where?
**Security Issues:** Any warnings about malware, hacking, or unsafe content?

blocks.text: Search Console shows you exactly how Google sees your site. If a page isn't indexed, it cannot rank — and you wouldn't know without checking here.
8. Analytics
Can you answer these questions right now, without guessing?

items: How many visitors did your website get last month?
Which pages do people look at most?
Where is your traffic coming from — Google, social media, direct?
What percentage of visitors contact you?

blocks.text: If you can't answer these, you're running a business with no feedback loop. You can't improve what you don't measure.
Options: **Google Analytics 4** (free, powerful, complex to set up), **Plausible** (paid, simple, GDPR-friendly), **Fathom** (paid, very simple). Any of these is better than none.
If you have analytics installed, verify the tracking code is on **every** page of your site — not just the homepage. It's a common mistake that leads to wildly inaccurate data.
9. Broken Links
Broken links (pages that return a 404 error) frustrate visitors and waste your crawl budget — the quota Google uses to discover your content.
Use the free tool **brokenlinkcheck.com** or the Screaming Frog SEO Spider (free up to 500 URLs) to scan your site.
When you find broken links, fix them by:

items: Updating the link to the correct current URL
Setting up a 301 redirect from the old broken URL to the correct destination
Removing the link entirely if the content no longer exists

blocks.text: Pay particular attention to your footer, navigation menu, and any "Read more" or "Learn more" links in your content — these are the most commonly neglected and the most commonly broken when pages are renamed or deleted.
10. Security and Software Updates
If your website runs on WordPress, this is non-negotiable: log in and check the last time you updated your plugins, themes, and WordPress core.
WordPress powers 40% of the web and is the single most-targeted CMS for automated attacks. Outdated plugins are the number one entry point for hackers.
Check:

items: Are all plugins updated to the latest version?
Do you have plugins installed that you no longer use? (Deactivate and delete them — inactive plugins are still a security risk)
Is WordPress core on the latest version?
Do you have automated backups running and tested recently?
Has your security plugin flagged any issues in the last 30 days?

blocks.text: If you're on a modern stack without a plugin-based CMS — for example Next.js on Vercel — most of this section is irrelevant. There are no plugins to update, no admin panel to compromise, and no WordPress-specific attack surface.
Your Audit Score
Go through all 10 points and count how many you pass cleanly.

rows: Schedule the next audit in 90 days
Fix the failing points within 30 days
Prioritise speed, security, and forms immediately
This website is almost certainly costing you customers right now

blocks.text: What to Do When You Find Problems
Not all problems are equal. Here's the priority order:

items: **Fix first:** Broken contact forms, missing SSL, security vulnerabilities. These are immediate business risk.
**Fix soon:** Speed below 50, Core Web Vitals failures, broken links, missing analytics. These are eroding your traffic and conversions.
**Fix when you can:** Meta descriptions, analytics completeness, tablet layout. Important but not urgent.

blocks.text: If you find multiple problems and your site runs on WordPress, it's worth asking whether you're patching a fundamentally slow and complex platform, or whether a rebuild on modern infrastructure would be more efficient in the long run.
